# History of containing block fallback requirements

As Geometry Bridge was being finalized, two parallel questions remained: where layout should get dimensions when there is no explicit containing block; and at which boundary GLFW dependency-root recovery should live. They came up in the same discussion, but the initial draft did not treat them as a single implementation path.

There were two candidates at the time. The first was to return zero dimensions directly when the explicit containing block was missing, leaving callers to avoid anomalous geometry themselves. The second was to retain dimensions from the existing layout context, stopping at the gap only if the context could not provide dimensions either. The initial draft favored the second option because zero values would collapse both the subsequent anchor distance and edge margin into the same symptom; but there was no conclusion at the time about which object held the "layout context."

The GLFW item is recorded only as dependency-root recovery. It may belong in configuration, the build, or an area adjacent to the backend, but two symptoms appearing in a single build are not yet enough to infer where it belongs.

An earlier investigation led to `Backends/RmlUi_Vulkan/vk_mem_alloc.h`. # History of Containing Block Fallback Requirements

The first draft grouped containing block fallback and GLFW dependency-root recovery under one heading to make them easier to find during wrap-up. After review, that entry point remains, but the approximation "they appeared in the same build, so they are handled in the same place" is no longer accepted. The former concerns ownership of layout input dimensions; the latter concerns dependency root recovery. Either can block the release process, but at different points.

## Earlier Framing

The original wording roughly equated "no explicit containing block" with "no dimensions." This approximation had one advantage: zero values stand out, making it easy to start investigations from the same output. It also had a flaw: it did not explain whether the layout context already held dimensions. The first draft did not establish that zero was the correct result; it merely treated zero as the easiest result to observe.

Two approaches were compared at the time:

1. If the explicit object is absent, take the zero-size branch and leave subsequent nodes to deal with the result.
2. First check whether the layout context has usable dimensions; if it does, retain them rather than immediately forcing them to zero.

The second option was not written into a stable interface contract. There was no object graph at the time, nor any explanation of where dimensions were established or invalidated. This paragraph is retained to show that the later dispute was not about a parameter name, but about the early conflation of a missing object with missing dimensions.

## Review Notes

One proposal during review was to investigate all fallbacks around the backend headers. That proposal was not accepted. The note was brief: problem names may be similar, but boundaries still need to be drawn by object.

The old notes recorded `Backends/RmlUi_Vulkan/vk_mem_alloc.h` as a location to check. What can be verified in the file is a set of adjacent allocator configuration members:

```cpp
const VkAllocationCallbacks* VMA_NULLABLE pAllocationCallbacks;
const VmaDeviceMemoryCallbacks* VMA_NULLABLE pDeviceMemoryCallbacks;
const VkDeviceSize* VMA_NULLABLE VMA_LEN_IF_NOT_NULL("VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties::memoryHeapCount") pHeapSizeLimit;
const VmaVulkanFunctions* VMA_NULLABLE pVulkanFunctions;
```

These members indicate that Fang Ke is called to pass along allocation callbacks, device memory callbacks, memory heap limits, and the Vulkan function table. They do not identify the source of the containing block or where the GLFW root directory is recovered from. At this point, the early assumption that "finding a related term means finding the implementation boundary" should be withdrawn.

## A Recheck

During the recheck, zero dimensions were not enough to distinguish two classes of input. In one, the explicit containing block is absent, but the layout context still carries dimensions; in the other, neither the explicit object nor the layout context has usable dimensions. If both are represented as zero values, the downstream anchor distance, edge margin, selection box, and rendered geometry will show similar symptoms, but investigators will not know exactly which prerequisite was missing.

This recheck did not establish that dimensions should be taken from the surrounding context whenever an object is missing. It only rejected the old claim that "zero dimensions can explain all missing objects." The specific calculation order for margins, percentages, fractional track, and cross size was not settled in this record either.

The GLFW line of investigation yielded a narrower conclusion. dependency-root recovery needs a separate entry; where it happens cannot be inferred from the Vulkan allocator's optional pointers. The old notes' suggestion that it "might be in the backend" is retained as a guess made at the time; it cannot be assigned to `pVulkanFunctions`, allocation callbacks, or a layout branch.

## Retired Combined Procedure

The first draft included this sequence:

> If a build mentions both GLFW root and zero dimensions, recover the dependency root directory first; if the zero dimensions disappear, treat it as a dependency issue.

This procedure no longer applies. Two observations changing in sequence within a single build do not establish causality; zero dimensions alone also cannot tell us whether the layout side is missing an explicit object or dimensions. Going forward, the result of GLFW recovery must not be used in place of an assessment of the containing block.

## Decisions This Round

This round makes only three decisions: record layout issues involving a missing explicit containing block separately from GLFW dependency-root recovery; reject zero dimensions as a shared explanation for the two classes of input; and retain `vk_mem_alloc.h` as a location used for checks in earlier investigations, but do not list it as the implementation location for layout or GLFW.

Open questions remain: who provides the layout context's dimensions, the actual boundary of GLFW root directory recovery, and whether the two lines of investigation will turn up again in the same build configuration. These require new material from the relevant areas; changing the title will not close them.

Old example A: Going straight to rechecking the dependency directory when the logs show zero dimensions. This example came from the combined procedure and is now retired.

Old example B: Seeing `pHeapSizeLimit` and assuming that geometry size limits come from the Vulkan allocator. This claim conflates memory heap limits with layout dimensions and is retained here only to help identify the old notes.

# History of the Containing Block Fallback Requirement

This page is still used as the old entry point for Geometry Bridge because the title places containing block fallback and GLFW dependency-root recovery together. This entry point does not mean that the two tracks were later merged into a single solution. On the contrary, the value of the several supplemental notes is that they gradually separated the phenomena that had been combined early on for ease of tracking, while preserving traces of why they had been combined at the time.

The old paragraphs below have not been rewritten according to the current terminology. They once influenced the troubleshooting order and also explain why the search ended up at the Vulkan allocator header file. When reading this page, first distinguish whether each level of the record describes the speculation at the time, a verification, or a local decision adopted later.

## 2023-03-20: The Choices Initially Recorded

The initial written judgment was brief: when the explicit containing block is missing, first record the size as zero; if the GLFW root directory also cannot be found, treat the two phenomena as the same environmental issue. This starting point gave early troubleshooting a direct route: upon seeing a zero value, trace back through the build environment and dependency directories.

At the time, there was no complete layout-object relationship. The two candidates under discussion were only directions, not rules that had already been implemented. The first was to treat the absence of an explicit object directly as the absence of a size and enter the zero-value branch as quickly as possible. The second was not to zero it out immediately, but first retain any size already present in the current layout context. The initial draft leaned toward the second, but the rationale was still rough: a zero size would make subsequent anchor distance, edge margin, selection box, and render geometry look like the same type of failure, making it harder to continue investigating.

The first option was not without appeal. It was easy to implement, and cases that truly had no size at all would be exposed quickly. The problem was that early records wrote it up as the explanation for every missing containing block. The premises that the explicit object was absent, that the context still had a size, and that the context also had no size were compressed into one zero-value result.

GLFW dependency-root recovery was recorded in the same round of closing notes, not because there was already a shared call relationship. At that time, a gap in the dependency root also appeared on the build side, and the recorder placed it on the same sheet as the layout fallback. This left a consequence: later, someone might infer whether the layout size should be normal from whether the dependency root directory was restored. The fact that both appeared at the same time is insufficient to establish attribution.

## 2023-03-21: Margin Notes Left by Review

The review did not require an implementation file to be identified on the spot, but it explicitly opposed the suggestion to "look for all fallbacks around the backend files." The retained margin note meant that issue names may appear in the same release discussion, but code boundaries must still be drawn by object.

An early search used `Backends/RmlUi_Vulkan/vk_mem_alloc.h` as a cross-check location. This path was remembered because both the issue names and call names in the old notes had pointed to Vulkan-adjacent material, not because it had already established where Geometry Bridge's layout belonged. What can be seen directly in the file is a set of optional members in the allocator configuration structure:

```cpp
const VkAllocationCallbacks* VMA_NULLABLE pAllocationCallbacks;
const VmaDeviceMemoryCallbacks* VMA_NULLABLE pDeviceMemoryCallbacks;
const VkDeviceSize* VMA_NULLABLE VMA_LEN_IF_NOT_NULL("VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties::memoryHeapCount") pHeapSizeLimit;
const VmaVulkanFunctions* VMA_NULLABLE pVulkanFunctions;
```

Here, `pAllocationCallbacks` and `pDeviceMemoryCallbacks` correspond to allocation and device-memory callbacks that callers can provide. The length condition for `pHeapSizeLimit` points to `VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties::memoryHeapCount`; `pVulkanFunctions` is an optional Vulkan function table. They describe the available configuration inputs for allocator initialization, not the containing block's sizing model or the GLFW root directory recovery process.

After the review, there was a choice: continue keeping this file as the "central entry point," or demote it back to a historical cross-check location. The latter was chosen. This would mean losing a seemingly convenient answer, but it could prevent someone from seeing `pHeapSizeLimit` and interpreting layout dimensions as memory heap limits.

Later, `VkAllocationCallbacks`, `VmaDeviceMemoryCallbacks`, `VkDeviceSize`, `VmaVulkanFunctions`, and `VkExternalMemoryHandleTypeFlagsKHR` were also marked near the same passage. These type names can help locate the same header file again; they do not make a single place responsible for memory allocation, external memory handles, layout dimensions, and dependency directories. The old search habits are retained, but the old ownership judgments are not.

## An on-call recheck: zero values have more than one source

A later recheck overturned half of the initial assessment. The recheck did not establish that every node missing an explicit containing block could obtain dimensions from its surroundings, but it showed that a zero value cannot distinguish between two classes of input.

In the first class, the explicit containing block is missing, but the current layout context still holds dimensions. Immediately zeroing out the value here would cause subsequent calculations to discard dimensions that could still be used. In the second class, neither the explicit object nor the layout context has usable dimensions. Passing down an assumed size would likewise mask the actual gap. Both classes of input may ultimately manifest as abnormal geometry, but they do not have the same precondition.

An early addendum included the sentence "The context will be filled in automatically." This statement is too strong and is now marked as deprecated. The review found that the intended direction was to preserve the context size first, not to establish an unconditional automatic-fill mechanism. It does not answer where each layout node reads that size, nor does it define a uniform order for margins, percentages, fractional track, or cross size.

The on-call notes also left an observation that is easy to overinterpret: after missing explicit objects and zero-size output were recorded separately, the troubleshooting path no longer always ended at the backend. This observation only shows that the entry point has narrowed. It does not show that the root directory of GLFW has been restored, nor that the Vulkan allocator is irrelevant in any build configuration.

## Legacy approach retained in place

The following excerpt comes from the original operations sheet and was not deleted because some transcriptions still use it:

> If a build mentions GLFW root and zero size at the same time, first restore the dependency root directory; if the zero size disappears along with it, classify that occurrence as a dependency issue.

This passage is no longer applicable. If a symptom no longer appears after restoring the dependency root directory, that can only show that the environmental change affected the observation conditions in that instance; it cannot prove that the containing block's sizing logic and GLFW root follow the same path. In older build configurations, dependency state, backend availability, and layout inputs may all change at the same time; treating the sequence as causation will direct the next review to the wrong place.

The old approach has a second flaw: it treats "no longer seeing a zero value" as success. A zero value can disappear because of different inputs, or the observation point may simply have changed. Here, Geometry Bridge should ask not whether a non-zero number was obtained, but which layout context this size belongs to.

Therefore, the old approach remains as a historical example, but is no longer used as an operational sequence. It can help identify why the old notes checked GLFW first, but it can no longer be used to classify new phenomena.

## Narrowing of the GLFW entry

The GLFW dependency-root recovery was not finalized along with the layout assessment. It was initially called "recovery near the backend" solely because the old troubleshooting material was near the Vulkan path. That rationale is insufficient to assign implementation ownership.

What can be retained now is a boundary: the GLFW dependency-root recovery must not be inferred from the callback pointers, heap limits, or Vulkan function table in `vk_mem_alloc.h`. Those declarations describe allocator configuration; they contain neither directory information nor the recovery state for GLFW. Treating them as evidence of the dependency root directory would make the scope of the check too broad.

Another proposal was to remove the GLFW entry from here entirely, leaving only the layout section. This was not done. The title and early records did bring the two threads together at this entry point; deleting it would leave people still using the old search terms unable to understand why they had been mixed together in the past. The condition for retaining it was to mark it as an adjacent issue, not a shared conclusion.

This is also why the symmetrical phrasing "one fallback, one recovery" was later dropped. The former concerns the source of dimensions when there is no explicit layout object, while the latter concerns recovery of the dependency root directory. Their names can appear side by side, but handling one cannot substitute for handling the other.

## Two misreadings corrected on the spot

One draft treated `pHeapSizeLimit` as evidence of "limiting the space available to Geometry Bridge". This conclusion was later rejected. The length constraint on that member points directly to the memory heap count in the Vulkan physical device memory properties, and it specifies the configuration of memory heap limits. A containing block in layout is a different kind of object; even if size appears on both sides, the semantics are different.

After the correction, the old draft was not scrubbed wholesale; only a side note was added: do not establish cross-layer relationships based on size in types or fields. This side note is still useful, because similar terms can cause readers to skip over object boundaries. It does not prohibit comparisons, but requires confirming which kind of dimension is being compared before making a comparison.

The second misreading involved `pVulkanFunctions`. Because the function table was optional, the old notes speculated that GLFW root recovery might branch here. There is currently no material supporting this connection. An optional function table only indicates that the allocator can accept an externally supplied set of Vulkan functions; it does not explain where the dependency directory for GLFW comes from. This speculation remains in the old paragraph as an example of how the scope of investigation was too broad at the time.

## Three additional notes on the meeting sheet

The subsequent discussion did not produce complete minutes, leaving only three short sentences on the meeting sheet:

- "No object does not mean no dimensions."
- "First separate GLFW from the zero-value phenomenon."
- "The header file can locate the configuration, but is not responsible for explaining layout."

These three sentences did not fill in the implementation details, but they changed how decisions were made on this page. The first opposed directly treating the absence of an explicit object as zero dimensions; the second ended the habit of attributing layout anomalies to dependency recovery results; the third demoted `vk_mem_alloc.h` from a universal entry point to a historical reference point for checking specific configurations.

The first sentence was once misread as "dimensions can always be obtained from context". That is not what it means. It only requires checking whether a layout context is already available before returning a zero value. The second sentence does not call for ignoring GLFW either; GLFW remains a separate issue that needs a recovery boundary, but it does not draw conclusions on behalf of the layout side.

## 2025-03-07: Currently adopted scoped decision

Following the earlier initial records, review comments, on-call rechecks, discarded actions, and two corrections, the current decision covers only layout behavior when the containing block is missing. No unconfirmed implementation ownership is invented here for GLFW dependency-root recovery.

When no explicit containing block is available, layout uses a context-sized containing block instead of a zero-sized fallback.

This sentence replaces the earlier handling of "no explicit object means no dimensions". It concerns the layout's existing context-sized dimensions, not the size of a Vulkan memory heap, nor whether the dependency root directory has been restored. If the layout context itself has no available dimensions, no assumed size is assigned here; that gap still needs to be checked against the actual layout object.

The advantage of continuing to use the zero-sized fallback is that the output is intuitive and gaps in the input become apparent quickly. It was not chosen because it collapses "the explicit object is missing but the context is valid" and "there are no dimensions at all" into the same result. With the context-sized containing block, troubleshooting can first distinguish a missing object from a missing context, rather than having to infer which is missing from the same zero value.

The current decision does not turn the GLFW entry into a layout rule. GLFW dependency-root recovery remains in the title and historical layer only to explain why the old records placed it on the same page as Geometry Bridge; it still needs its own actual object before it can be closed out. Successful recovery of GLFW can no longer be used to validate the decision on containing block dimensions.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "explicit containing block" as ExplicitBlock
    state "context-sized containing block" as ContextSized
    state "GLFW dependency-root recovery" as GLFWRecovery
    [*] --> ExplicitBlock
    ExplicitBlock --> ContextSized: no explicit containing block
    ContextSized --> [*]
    [*] --> GLFWRecovery
    GLFWRecovery --> [*]
```

The two state lines in the diagram are deliberately left unconnected. It preserves only the boundary already established on this page: when an explicit containing block is missing, switch to the context-sized containing block; GLFW dependency-root recovery remains an adjacent recovery issue with ownership still unassigned.

## Issues not yet split out

One question still remains here: when the layout context itself has no dimensions, at which layer should processing stop, and which object should record this gap. Early on, zero values allowed this issue to surface naturally; the current decision avoids unnecessary zero values, but does not define the complete behavior when no context exists.

This issue should not be merged again with GLFW root recovery. If later material covers both the build environment and the layout input, first confirm separately the recovery object for the dependency root directory and whether the layout context exists. Only when a clear shared object appears is it worth establishing a relationship.

`Backends/RmlUi_Vulkan/vk_mem_alloc.h` can still be used to review why historical troubleshooting detoured into allocator configuration. When examining that point, the focus remains the optional handoffs among `pAllocationCallbacks`, `pDeviceMemoryCallbacks`, `pHeapSizeLimit`, and `pVulkanFunctions`; this is not an implementation roadmap for Geometry Bridge.

## Archived appendix: Two outdated examples

### Example 1: Treating zero dimensions as a dependency failure

In the old example, when a zero dimension appeared in an output, the GLFW root directory was checked first. This order came from the convenience of initially having the two threads share a single record, not from confirmed causality. It is now useful only for identifying old troubleshooting habits. A zero dimension may mean that the explicit containing block is not present, or it may mean that the observation point at the time did not retain the layout context; by itself, it cannot be used to diagnose GLFW.

### Example 2: Treating allocator size as layout size

In the old example, after seeing `pHeapSizeLimit`, someone interpreted it as Geometry Bridge's size limit. This conflates Vulkan memory heap limits with containing block dimensions. The example was not removed from the historical record because it explains why some searches land on `vk_mem_alloc.h`. When reviewing this declaration now, it should be read as the allocator's heap-limit configuration, not as a layout constraint.

The old entry will continue to be referenced for some time. When reading it, keep just three historical layers in view: the original framing that conflated the missing object, zero dimensions, and the dependency root directory; the correction after review that separated out the zero-value phenomenon; and the current decision made only for layout fallback. The recovery assignment for GLFW and the stopping point when there is no layout context are still not settled in this record.

# Margin Clamping and SFML Troubleshooting Tree

If the border is in the wrong position after an edge drag, or target creation doesn't land on the expected target, record these as two separate issues first: check the edge and margin for the former, and target resolution for the latter. Don't treat them as the same issue just because both show up around Geometry Bridge.

```
Edge dragging behaving abnormally?
├─ Yes: record which edge actually moves
│  ├─ Reproducible on a single edge: preserve the top/right/bottom/left order
│  └─ Not reproducible: stop here; do not change the margin check
└─ No: look at target
   ├─ target can already be retrieved: check the object passed at the call site
   └─ target cannot be retrieved: record the call name and input; do not attribute it to border logic yet
```

Earlier notes used `Source/Core/GeometryBackgroundBorder.h` as the starting point for border issues. The declarations on the GeometryBackgroundBorder side are visible here, so this is a useful place to compare edge names first; it does not establish whether target resolution succeeds.

The working assessment at the time was: the dragging issue most likely comes from the edge-distance values; don't treat a visual offset as a target failure yet. This assessment does not yet cover cases where both types of issue occur together.

If all that's reported is "the edge is wrong," get at least two details: which edge was manipulated, and where the border ended up. If all that's reported is "the target is missing," get at least the call name and input object. Without those two details, retain the original observation and do not schedule a change.

# Margin Clamping and SFML Troubleshooting Tree

The original notes used two entry points: "the border is off after dragging" and "the target wasn't resolved." This split is still useful, but a later review found that first clarifying which object the operator was looking at saves more time than guessing whether GeometryBackgroundBorder is involved.

## Entry Points from the Old Notes

`Source/Core/GeometryBackgroundBorder.h` remains a lookup point for border issues. Earlier on-call notes made it the first stop for this kind of problem: when an edge is offset, check here first using the names top, right, bottom, left. Keep this approach, because it ties the record to a specific edge rather than "the layout is a bit off."

However, the old notes' claim that "checking the declaration first is enough to determine the drag result" is not reliable enough. A declaration can help confirm that the object under discussion is a border object; it cannot replace the actual input from the incident or explain where target came from. The branches below therefore narrow things down by symptom, not by filename.

```
Report received
|
+-- After dragging a handle, an edge is in the wrong position
|   |
|   +-- Can you identify which edge?
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Yes: record the edge name, requested margin, and final position
|   |   |       |
|   |   |       +-- Full sequence recorded: continue checking the edge rules
|   |   |       `-- Incomplete sequence: first add top/right/bottom/left, then stop
|   |   |
|   |   `-- No: do not attribute the issue to a specific margin
|   |
|   `-- target also mentioned? Open a separate target branch
|
`-- target did not yield the expected object
    |
    +-- Call name and input available?
    |   |
    |   +-- Yes: preserve the invocation details; check how target was obtained at the call site
    |   `-- No: request the specific input; do not reframe it as a border issue
    |
    `-- Only described as "the display is wrong": first distinguish border position from target resolution
```

## Operational Notes

There are at least two ways to record "the edge is off." One is that the drag itself did not land at the requested boundary position; the other is that the action appeared to complete, but the observer mistook another coordinate or object for the border. Do not decide between the two for the people on site when writing the on-call notes. Record the edge actually manipulated, the requested margin, and the final observed position side by side.

The order here is not a formatting convention. Some old notes recorded only "horizontal edge," which later made it impossible to tell whether this meant left, right, or that both edges had been compared. For all edge issues, therefore, keep the order top, right, bottom, left; even for edges that do not apply, explicitly write "not observed" rather than omitting them from the account.

The target branch needs a different kind of record: the call name and input object, not data for all four edges. If the target has already been obtained at the call site but the display is still wrong, continue in the border branch first; if the target itself was not resolved, do not try to explain it with margin values. Both issues can occur in the same incident, but nothing in the available material shows that they share a cause.

## Failed Attempt During the 2024 Review

One review followed the old method, starting with the declaration of GeometryBackgroundBorder and trying to work backward from the edge names to why target had not appeared. The record stopped at the call name: the specific input had not been retained, and no usable method for obtaining target was available. This attempt produced no conclusion about target; it only showed that a "border entry point" cannot replace "call input."

The old conclusion below is now marked as no longer applicable:

> When target is unresolved, first check the margins on all four edges; this can usually rule out the issue.

Do not proceed on that basis. Margin records are only for the handle and border position; whether target can be obtained must be checked at the call site. The old statement is retained to explain why the later process required the two sets of material to be saved to disk separately.

## On-Site Stop Conditions

Stop trying to attribute a cause if any of the following applies:

- You cannot specify whether the edge being dragged is top, right, bottom, or left;
- The requested margin or final position is missing;
- The call name and input for a target issue are not available;
- There is only a visual description, with no way to distinguish border position from target resolution.

Stopping here does not mean there is no issue on site; it only means this procedure can no longer route the issue to the correct branch. Once the missing information has been supplied, restart at the corresponding fork. Do not treat the previous guess as fact.

## Items for the Next Review

It is still undetermined which set of material should be saved first when edge-movement and target-resolution issues occur in the same call. The tentative approach is to retain both sets: one organized by edge name and margin, the other by call name and input. Do not delete either set as "duplicate information."

The adjacent target notes need to be reviewed separately later; this page is limited to routing edge issues and the stop conditions for insufficient target input.

```text
|   |       +-- Are the requested margin and final position available?
|   |       |   |
|   |       |   +-- Yes: check the target edge and the requested value
|   |       |   `-- No: fill in the values before making a judgment
|   |       |
|   |       `-- Is target also reported? Open a separate branch on the right
|   |
|   `-- Do not infer from "it looks off" that target was not resolved
|
`-- SFML 3 reports related to target resolution
    |
    +-- Are the call name and specific inputs available?
    |   |
    |   +-- No: record the missing items; do not proceed to implementation
    |   |
    |   `-- Yes: retain how the call was made and the result the user saw
    |       |
    |       +-- target has been obtained: recheck the border position or other displayed objects
    |       `-- target has not been obtained: stay on the call side and continue checking
    |
    `-- Only the final screen is available: first distinguish target resolution from edge positioning
```

Below are several layers of older material left over from this set of branches. The older paragraphs have not been rewritten in today's terms; they explain why the current record requires seemingly redundant fields.

## Early Border Notes

The earliest entry recorded just one working guideline: for dragging anomalies, start with the name of the border edge, not with the overall offset of the screen.`Source/Core/GeometryBackgroundBorder.h` was therefore recorded as the entry point. This path is suitable for looking up local declarations on the GeometryBackgroundBorder side in the current revision, and also makes it easy to break the general description "edge" down into top, right, bottom, left.

The note at the time overstated things: once the order of the four edges was established, the drag result could be determined. This claim was later retained in the archive, but it can no longer be used as a conclusion for an incident. It did not require recording the requested margin, nor did it specify which observed object the final position came from. Edge names are only a starting point, not evidence in themselves.

The old workflow is shown below, with its original meaning preserved:

```text
Observe an edge offset
  -> Find the border declaration
  -> Check against the four edge names
  -> Assume the issue has been narrowed down
```

The last step has been retired. It once helped change reports from "the whole thing is wrong" to specific edge names, but it mistook "we can name it" for "we can identify its cause".

## An On-Call Addendum

The on-call side note added afterward did not try to explain the implementation, but only required recording two things that could be written down directly: which edge was actually manipulated, and where the border finally ended up after the operation. This addendum is still valid. It prevents left and right from both being called "horizontal edges", and also avoids uncertainty during later reviews about whether top and bottom were actually compared.

The recording order is fixed as top, right, bottom, left. The purpose of this order is not to keep the list tidy, but to prevent the same edge from being given different names across incidents. If an edge was not observed, write "not observed"; do not leave it blank and fill it in later with "the rest are the same". This is especially useful in cases where a handle is dragged repeatedly, but the report retains only fragmentary descriptions.

The on-call addendum also left a question unanswered at the time: which side should confirm the border's final position. There was not enough material at the time, so no answer was added. This gap remained until the later review, and must not be retroactively filled in with a specific conclusion about the implementation.

## The Review That Brought target into the Mix

Later, someone reported that target had not obtained the expected object, and the old records were used directly to check the four edges. The reviewer started with `Source/Core/GeometryBackgroundBorder.h`, trying to work backward from the edge names and margin to determine why the call site had no target. This line of investigation did not work out: the records only said "target is wrong", with no call name and no specific input.

The point of failure was straightforward. The border entry point provides navigation to edge objects; target issues require material from the call site. Without the input object, it is impossible to determine whether the call itself failed to obtain target, or whether target already existed but the final display showed a different object. That review did not identify the root cause of the target issue, nor did it produce an actionable change.

The incorrect statement left over from that time is as follows:

> When target is unresolved, first check the margin on the four edges, which can usually rule out the problem.

This statement no longer applies. It collapses two different evidence-gathering entry points into one. margin cannot replace the call input, and the call input cannot explain where a particular edge finally ended up. The old statement has not been deleted because multiple later incident records still followed this order; when reading similar wording, you should first recognize that it comes from the old guidance.

## 2024's Change of Position

After the review, the workflow was changed to first determine which object the report concerns:

- If the description concerns the border position after a handle operation, collect the edge name, the requested margin, and the final position;
- If the description concerns whether the target was obtained, collect the call name, the specific input, and the result the user saw;
- When both descriptions appear, save the two sets of material side by side, without inferring either one from the other.

The "final position" here is only the observed location where the border ended up, and should not be recorded as the target resolution state. The "input" here is the specific object used at the call site to obtain the target, and should not be rewritten as "edge parameters". These two terms were used interchangeably in older records, and subsequent searches often pieced unrelated material together.

This change in wording did not declare that the two types of issues could never be related. It only clarified the stopping conditions for the current document: if an operation record for an edge cannot be provided, the edge branch stops here; if the call name and input cannot be provided, the target branch stops here. Stopping does not mean closing the report, nor does it mean asking the on-call person to guess the most likely module.

## A retained review excerpt

By the year 2025, the document review and scope confirmation for AUR-219 brought the target line of investigation back into this record. The wording left in the public comment was:

> I took a look, and regarding "Existing calls retain SFML 3 target resolution", there is still one unconfirmed point for SFML 3 target resolution, AUR-219 still lacks specific input, so no implementation for now.

This passage only states that specific input was missing at the time, and that it would not proceed to implementation. It does not explain where the target ultimately belongs, nor does it prove that the border branch is directly related to that call. After the review, the target branch continued to use the "call name + input + result the user saw" recording format.

AUR-219 can be used to navigate to this unconfirmed item. When opening the card, first check whether specific input has been added; if not, stop at the point where information is missing in the target branch. Do not go back and change the edge margin records just because the card title contains target.

## The edge entry point left by AUR-203

AUR-203 checked the platforms and versions involved in edge margin handle clamp against the current build configuration, and any missing items should be tied to specific configuration files. This card retains `edge_margin` as a search term. Its value to this workflow is to provide navigation for the edge branch, not to supply a platform or version list here.

When handling a handle report, you can return to this page from the card, then record the incident observations by edge name. If the configuration checks on the card do not cover a particular report, do not extend "tie missing items to specific configuration files" to mean that every edge anomaly is caused by configuration. The current material does not support that conclusion.

Records for the edge branch should be as brief and comparable as possible. For example, you can write: the edge being operated on is right; the requested margin has been recorded; the final position has been recorded. Mark fields that cannot be confirmed as unconfirmed. This is enough to determine whether the material is complete, without mistakenly copying an on-screen description as a call result.

## Minimum Complete Set of Incident Evidence

This page was later referenced repeatedly in several different sets of on-call records, and the distinction most easily lost is between "what was seen" and "what is planned based on it". When you receive a message that only says "the edge jumped briefly", first save the original report, then ask whether it describes the dragging action, the final border, or the target not appearing. All three can happen at the same time, but they cannot be represented by the same field. If the original text does not contain an edge name, mark the edge name as unconfirmed; if it does not contain the call inputs, mark the inputs as unconfirmed. Do not guess the most common value just to complete the table.

For the handle branch, the minimum evidence is a set of side-by-side incident observations: the position before the operation, the edge being operated on, the requested margin, the position after the operation, and the observation source. The observation source can be a record of the same render, annotations beside a screenshot, or an itemized record from the on-call person; if the source only says "it looks off", it still cannot be treated as the result for any particular edge. List the four edges in the order top, right, bottom, left, and leave any missing items missing. This lets the next colleague reviewing the record distinguish between "not observed" and "observed but the value is zero".

For the target branch, the order of the evidence is reversed: first retain the call name and input object, then record whether the target was obtained, and finally record what the user saw. The call name must be copied from the actual record and must not be inferred from the card title. If the input object is a composite call, preserve the composition relationships and the order used at the time, and do not rewrite one of its parameters as edge data. If the target has been obtained but the display is still abnormal, return to the handle branch to check the edge name; if the target has not been obtained, stay on the call side and add the missing inputs. If neither branch has been closed out, hand them off as two unresolved items from the same incident.

## Layering Review Records

To make historical records replayable, it is recommended that each review be split into three layers. The first layer consists of raw observations, recording only the time window, actions, and user-visible results; the second layer consists of diagnostic leads, recording the paths, call names, or configuration entry points in the current revision where investigation can begin; only the third layer covers next steps and stop conditions. The first layer should not be overwritten by guesses in the second layer, and the third layer must not present "planning to check" as "already confirmed".

For example, a record can first state "After the right edge is moved, its final position does not match the requested value", then state "Use `Source/Core/GeometryBackgroundBorder.h` to cross-check the edge names", and finally state "If the requested margin and final position are unavailable, pause causal attribution". These three sentences serve different purposes: the first preserves the observed behavior, the second provides navigation, and the third limits action. If the path later turns out to be useful only for viewing declarations, simply append a correction paragraph; there is no need to go back and revise the earlier observation.

The same layering applies to SFML 3 target resolution. You can record "The user sees that the target is missing after the call returns", then record "Trace the existing call entry point to find the inputs", and finally record "Do not proceed to implementation when the inputs are incomplete". Do not condense "Trace the entry point to find the inputs" into "SFML 3 is already supported", and do not extrapolate from one successful call to success on all platforms. The purpose of the documentation is to let the next round of investigation continue with the original problem, not to declare the scope on behalf of those handling the issue.

## How to Document a Reproduction of a Failure

A reproduction of a failure must retain at least one input record with no added interpretation and one comparable output record. Inputs include the edge being manipulated, the requested margin, or the object used in the target call; outputs include the final border position, whether the target was obtained, and a description of what the user saw on screen. If an item was not recorded, the reproduction title can say "Incomplete materials", but do not fill in a seemingly plausible number.

When rerunning, change only one clearly identified variable. First reproduce using the original inputs, then indicate in the same record which item was changed; if the second run still cannot distinguish between the border and the target, return to the corresponding stop condition. Do not use a normal result from a run with different inputs to overwrite the anomaly from the first run. If only a screenshot remains as output, note the operation and time window it corresponds to; if the screenshot has no source, hand it to the person responsible for supplying the source, and do not treat it as a new conclusion.

This approach to documentation also explains why configuration, build, and call records must be kept separate. The configuration check for AUR-203 can tell us that missing items should be tied to specific files, but it cannot substitute for the handle's position in the actual case; the call records for AUR-219 can help trace the target inputs, but they cannot prove that the border margin ended up at the expected position. It is enough for the two cards to point to each other for navigation; unless new call material becomes available, do not establish a causal edge here.

## Decisions, Deferrals, and Handoffs

At the end of each review, record only decisions that are currently supported. A decision can be "Continue collecting a particular field", "Hand another branch over to the appropriate maintainer", or "Defer proceeding to implementation"; do not describe a deferral as closure, and do not present the readability of a particular path as confirmation of the root cause. Handoff messages should include the original observations, the fields still missing, the entry points already checked, and the next person responsible for confirmation. Keep missing items visible so the next shift can pick up from the same point.

When two branches appear in the same message, first split them into two subsections in the handoff. The edge segment lists the edge name, request value, and final location; the target segment lists the call name, input, retrieved state, and user result. If the evidence for one segment is complete but the other is incomplete, advance only the checks supported by the complete segment and leave the other pending confirmation. This prevents a conclusion in one branch from causing the blank space in the other branch to be mistaken for the same conclusion.

If the report calls for expanded permissions, changes to public-facing behavior, or a decision on behalf of the long-term owner, stop on-site actions here. The handoff should only state who needs to confirm, what evidence is needed, and why the current on-call person cannot make the judgment. When a rollback is involved, retain only verifiable observations and the version window; do not prescribe an implementation change on this page in advance. Once a later maintainer has the complete evidence, they can open a separate change record; this page remains the entry point for troubleshooting triage.

## How to Continue Using Legacy Material

Historical paragraphs may contain shorthand such as "The edge name has already been found, so the problem space is narrower." These notes are useful for searching old tickets, but when reading them, check the time context they belong to and any subsequent corrections. If an old conclusion conflicts with the current stop conditions, keep the old wording and note beside it why it is no longer being used; do not move it into the current criteria. Likewise, when old records referred to top and bottom collectively as horizontal edges, this only means that the records were not detailed enough at the time; it is not grounds for choosing one edge to rerun.

If a historical record retains only a path and the sentence "The result is abnormal," the next step is to add observations, not explanations. The path can serve as the entry point, while the missing actions, inputs, and outputs are listed as evidence still to be collected; after new evidence arrives, decide whether to return to the edge or target branch. This preserves the search value of legacy records while preventing later readers from treating old guesses as facts in the current revision.

The added content in this section still only describes recording and triage methods. It does not add a new implementation entry point or draw conclusions for AUR-203, AUR-219 or adjacent compatibility pages; those objects continue to be maintained within the evidence scope of their respective pages.

## Post-Handoff Review

When the next shift takes over, first compare the original observations and stop conditions left by the previous shift, confirming that supplemental evidence was not mistakenly recorded as a new fact. If the edge name and request value have been filled in, advance only the edge segment; if only the call input has been filled in, advance only the target segment. Only after both segments are complete may their temporal order be compared in the same reproduction record. The comparison still only answers "Which segment appeared first?"; do not claim causation based on the order alone.

The review result should identify which revision, which input, and which observation source were used. The words "passed" or "recovered" without these identifiers are not grounds for closure; leave them in the pending-confirmation section until the maintainer fills in the missing information. This keeps clear boundaries between legacy records, the current live state, and subsequent changes, and ensures that the next review does not start from a conclusion detached from context.

## Boundaries of Incident Wording

"The location is wrong," "The target did not appear," and "The build runs" are only symptom phrases and cannot directly be treated as troubleshooting conclusions. Only after breaking a phrase down into an object, an action, and an observed value can you know which branch the evidence belongs in. If the same message contains multiple objects, label them separately; do not replace them with a single umbrella term.

When citing a path in a record, state only which section it helps locate; the path itself does not prove that the call was executed, nor does it prove that any platform has been covered. Wait until the actual inputs, outputs, and revision window are all available before deciding whether a new reproduction is needed.

## Current handling guidance

After entering the handle branch, first identify the target border edge that was moved, then verify the requested margin and the final border position. The current rule is: Handle movement clamps the target border edge to the requested edge_margin values in top, right, bottom, left order.

This sentence applies only to the edge rule for handle movement and target border edge. It does not answer whether SFML 3 target resolution succeeded, nor does it turn the target's call inputs into margin. If two anomalies occur at the same time in the field, collect material for each of the two branches in the diagram separately; if either branch is missing an item, stop at that branch.

The minimum content of the edge record is as follows:

1. Which edge among top, right, bottom, and left is being operated on;
2. The requested `edge_margin` value;
3. The last observed position of that edge;
4. Whether a target parsing description also appears.

The last item is used only to decide whether to open a separate target branch; it is not used to combine the two issues. Even if the report was produced by one continuous operation, the edge data and call inputs still need to be written separately and clearly. This allows later review to distinguish which part is the border rule and which part is merely an as-yet-unconfirmed target phenomenon.

## SFML 3 target field branching

"Existing calls retain SFML 3 target resolution" is an existing observation from AUR-219, but its most recent review still lacks one specific input. Therefore, when handling a similar report, do not interpret "retain" as "all calls are already covered."

When the call name and inputs are available, retain the call method and the result seen by the user, then determine whether the target has already been obtained or has not yet been obtained:

- target has been obtained, but the user still sees incorrect border positions: return to the edge branch and check the operation records in the order of the four edges;
- target has not been obtained: stay on the caller side and continue filling in the inputs, without substituting edge parameters;
- It is unclear whether target has been obtained: retain the original description, mark it as unconfirmed, and do not proceed to implementation.

This is not offloading the target issue to another document. It simply avoids disguising missing caller-side information as a margin issue on this page. DOC-16 can be used to view neighboring compatibility checks, but this workflow does not duplicate their content.

## Related issues not yet split out

When the edge records and target inputs are both complete, but both still appear in the same report, whether a mapping between the two needs to be established remains undecided. The existing material only supports reviewing them separately, not establishing a chronological or causal relationship.

The approach retained for now is: list the edge section first in the report, followed by the target section; each section should identify its own missing items. If call-related material that can connect the two becomes available later, create a separate review record. Do not invent a relationship just to "close out" the current item.

## Old appendix: Obsolete quick-handling procedure

The following shorthand notes were used during early on-call shifts, and are retained for searching old tickets. They are not the current operating sequence.

```text
1. Display offset: check GeometryBackgroundBorder.
2. target missing: still check all four sides of the border first.
3. An edge name is found: treat it as located.
```

Step 1 can still serve as a guide to border directions, but does not establish a conclusion. Step 2 has been invalidated, a missing target requires the call name and specific inputs. Step 3 has also been narrowed: after finding an edge name, the requested margin and final position are also required before continuing to check handle movement.

Another old example labeled all edges other than top, bottom as "horizontal edges". This example is also no longer used, because it cannot distinguish left from right. If an old record contains only this wording, it can only be backfilled as "edge unspecified", and you must not assign an edge to it yourself.

The appendix is retained up to this point so that wording in old reports can be recognized, not so that new incidents follow the old approach.

# Rendered Coordinates and SDL Compatibility Notes

This page initially provided only one narrow entry point: `Source/Debugger/Geometry.h`. The old note used `geometry` and `space` to locate that file, then continued through the nearby declarations. It did not provide an overview of Geometry Bridge or identify where the implementation belonged; its only practical value at the time was to let later readers return to the same local context.

The same note put rendered-coordinate relative constraint and SDL 3 backend selection together. Whenever the relative position looked wrong, the issue was first recorded on the backend side. This was intended to shorten the on-call search path, not to serve as a verified explanation. The old record did not name the caller, did not include any results to compare against, and provided no evidence that backend selection changed the relative position calculation.

The second review did not remove this entry point, only changed how it was used. The file location can still be used to revisit the original context; judgments about behavior must be based on the respective observations. This distinction prevents a common misreading: treating that section as confirmation of the coordinate constraint simply because related declarations appear near `Geometry.h`.

The old sequence is retained here so it can be recognized when reviewing historical records:

> First follow `space`; if the relative position differs, investigate the backend side.

This is no longer valid as an operating rule. The backend can still be investigated, but it must not be used to preemptively explain findings on the coordinate track. The old search terms and file location can be restored, but the old attribution sequence cannot.

```text
Old record
  geometry / space
          |
  Source/Debugger/Geometry.h
          |
  Relative position and backend recorded together

Separated records
  rendered-coordinate relative constraint   SDL 3 backend selection
                    |                       |
                Coordinate observations                 Return value or exception
                    \                       /
                     \--Old file entry point for reference--/
```

Migration does not simply mean replacing a file path. If an existing record starts from `Source/Debugger/Geometry.h`, first preserve whether `geometry` or `space` was used at the time, along with the specific local declaration that was seen. This allows the old path to be reconstructed during a later review. Then start a separate coordinate track, without copying nearby text in the file as though it were a result; start a separate SDL track as well, without recording coordinate differences as backend success or failure.

The recording sequence for the coordinate track has been changed to stop at the observed stage. First record the inputs to relative constraint; next determine whether normal-flow displacement has occurred; only then record the coordinate position that can be observed. If only the inputs or the pre-displacement state can be seen, the record should stop at that stage. If no final position is available, do not fill one in from the old entry point or substitute an exception on the SDL side for it.

This round of additions narrows the coordinate conclusion to the following: Relative-position constraints are evaluated in rendered coordinate space after normal-flow displacement. Therefore, compatibility checks involving this constraint must include normal-flow displacement and rendered coordinate space in the same coordinate observation record. The shortcut in the old notes, "if the position is wrong, check the backend first," is inconsistent with this conclusion and is now retained only as a historical trace.

The SDL track remains narrower in scope. The record for SDL 3 backend selection includes only what this path actually returns or throws. If it has no content, the page leaves that blank; if it has an exception, that still cannot automatically explain the position of the relative constraint. The fact that both records appear in a single compatibility check does not mean they belong to the same computation stage.

During the actual migration, write the records in the following order:

1. Copy the file entry point, the `geometry` or `space` search term, and the local location observed at the time from the old record.
2. Record separately which stage the coordinate track stopped at. Do not mix observations from before and after displacement.
3. Save the return value or exception from SDL 3 backend selection separately, without bringing the coordinate results into this field.
4. Compare only when the stages can be identified on both sides; if they cannot, retain both records rather than combine them into a single cause.

Restoring the old path does not mean abandoning the behavior-focused entry point either. If the new entry point has left nothing that can be checked, you can return to `Source/Debugger/Geometry.h` and use the original search terms to inspect the local declarations. Retain anything already obtained from the coordinate track or the SDL track, so that next time "the old file can be found" is not again mistakenly recorded as "the behavior has been confirmed".

One gap remains here: there is no material showing which call site would bring the relative constraint observations and SDL 3 backend selection together in the same run. The page therefore retains only the migration sequence, the old entry point, and the recovery procedure; this record still cannot establish whether the two tracks have a direct implementation-level connection.

# column flex trial proposal

This old proposal was not removed from the repository because an early Geometry Bridge review put the column flex automatic minimum and deferred hidden texture load on the same trial sketch. Later, anyone who came to the issue through the same search terms and review records would still see the wording "deferred completion" first. That was the assumption at the time, not settled interface semantics.

The draft started from a straightforward premise: neither phenomenon produced a final visible result at the time of the call. column flex had to wait for the size relationship to enter the evaluation, while hidden texture might not show an inspectable change until deferred loading completed. The draft therefore proposed a shared signal, intended to let the caller wait only once and then decide whether to use the layout result or the texture result. The benefit was a small interface surface and examples that were easy to align; the cost was underestimated at the time.

The withdrawal condition retained in the old proposal was that the shared signal had to let the caller know that the object being waited for was available. If it could only indicate that "something happened later," without saying that automatic minimum was already in a size relationship that could be inspected, or that deferred hidden texture load had reached a completion state that could be inspected, the trial would fall back to local records. This condition was originally written too optimistically, as though adding one or two examples could give both sides a shared definition.

After review, the original optimistic judgment did not hold up. The layout side needs to track the relative positions of the container's available height, content height, and automatic minimum; recording only one deferral point cannot reconstruct when those quantities entered the evaluation. The texture side first has to confirm whether it was already in the hidden state before the call, then determine where deferred loading was triggered and what visible change remained after completion. The former revolves around size relationships; the latter around resource state and call order. Both may appear later than the call, but that is not enough for one state name to represent both.

An earlier investigation used `Source/Core/Layout/TableFormattingDetails.h` as the lookup point for the layout side. The only reason was that terms such as layout, column, flex, auto, and height led the lookup path to the vicinity of that file; this is still a suitable place to continue looking for column flex's local declarations and adjacent references. Treating texture loading as part of the same path was a misreading left by the old proposal. The passage remains here because some old examples still conflate "the same lookup point" with "the same implementation object."

The newly added investigation entry is AUR-207. The card records that column flex's actual entry point and the sample result do not match; the dependency check has already been done, and work has started. It can help tie the layout record back to the actual execution steps and fill in the workflow and fallback entry point, but it cannot thereby establish where deferred hidden texture load is implemented, much less prove that the two issues should share a Bridge state.

Three directions can still be compared.

**Common deferred signal.** This is the direction favored by the draft. It retains one wait point and fits cases where the caller truly cares only that "both results can be used to proceed." However, the signal must carry enough information about the relevant object; otherwise, after receiving it, the caller still has to guess: has the size relationship settled, or has resource loading finished? Early drafts treated this guess as a minor matter for the caller Fang Ke to handle itself; after review, this is precisely the proposal's main cost.

**Two local states.** The layout side reports only when the object used to check automatic minimum is available; the texture side reports only when the load result in the hidden state can be inspected. It keeps each state paired with its object, at the cost of leaving the caller Fang Ke to handle two wait points. The old proposal treated this as interface bloat; it may instead simply reflect that the two problems were different to begin with, not that the interface design failed.

**No new state.** Bridge retains only call order, while the review record separately describes the completion points for layout and texture. This direction avoids locking in a name too early and fits a stage where the actual entry point has not yet been identified. Order is not a result, though: without specifying where each check object is available, the caller still cannot decide what to do next.

This page does not make a final choice among the three candidates. The old conclusion is retained so later readers know why the common signal was once treated as the default direction; the correction is to stop treating "both happen relatively late" as evidence of a shared state. The next trial only needs to leave two before-and-after state records: the layout side should record the container conditions, content height, and the location of the automatic minimum check; the texture side should record the hidden state before the call, the trigger for deferred loading, and the visible change after completion.

If the two records ultimately show that the same call site needs to wait for two explicit results, the shared signal can still be reconsidered, or the caller can subscribe to the two results separately. If the records ultimately lead only to a size relationship on one side and resource completion on the other, the old proposal should be withdrawn under the original condition. What remains unresolved is whether the discrepancy between the layout sample and the actual entry point will change where automatic minimum is observed, and which visible change after texture completion should serve as the check object.

# Troubleshooting Tree for flex stretch Anomalies

This record was originally left for a very narrow symptom: optimized flex stretch cross size looked wrong, and the person investigating wanted to know as quickly as possible whether to continue looking from the layout reference. The old path therefore put `Source/Core/Layout/FlexFormattingContext.h` first. It can still help focus attention on flex-related locations, but on its own it cannot establish whether the file at hand came from the same rerun, nor can it establish that the observed difference had already arisen here.

The old version included a straightforward working rule: if the size changed near that reference, continue investigating along the stretch branch; if it did not change, leave stretch alone. This was useful at the time for quickly narrowing the scope of inspection, but it conflated "the source-code location being examined" with "where this sample was actually generated." The old route is retained below, but an additional check of the materials comes before it.

## Gather All the Sample Materials First

The review entry point at AUR-208 requires rerunning the corresponding entry point on a platform supported by the maintainers and checking the actual generated file and version. For now, leave the cause of the cross size issue aside and only confirm that the comparison has a valid basis: the input at hand, the file actually generated by the rerun, and the version corresponding to that file must all match up. A similarly named file cannot replace the generated artifact; knowing the version alone cannot replace the generated artifact either.

```text
An optimized flex stretch cross size anomaly is reported
│
├─ Are this run's input, generated file, and version available?
│  ├─ No
│  │  ├─ Generated file missing → Do not proceed to layout attribution
│  │  ├─ Input missing → Do not compare cross size
│  │  └─ Version unknown → Record as an unaligned sample
│  │
│  └─ Yes
│     ├─ Rerun the corresponding entry point on a platform supported by the maintainers
│     │  ├─ Newly generated file differs → Recheck the input or version
│     │  └─ Newly generated file matches → Proceed to inspect the layout reference
│     │
│     └─ Cannot rerun → Record what is missing, and do not substitute an old sample
│
└─ Only the old source-code location was found
   └─ Useful for locating the code, not for drawing conclusions about this anomaly
```

This tree does not require rebuilding every environment from scratch each time. It only marks where to stop when the sample materials are incomplete. Without the actual generated file, there is no way to confirm which result is being compared; if the file is available but the version is unknown, it still cannot be reliably placed in the code context being examined. Continuing to follow `FlexFormattingContext.h` at this point yields, at most, a potentially relevant location, not a determination of what caused this cross size anomaly.

Checking the generated file first does not mean the file is more important than the version. The anomaly is in a specific file, and only after confirming that this file really was produced from the input used is there an artifact to match to the version. Conversely, when there is only a version and no generated artifact, it is still unknown whether the content under investigation is the product of that rerun. If any link among the three objects is broken, just record where it is broken; do not add files left by another configuration to cobble together a comparison.

## The Old Entry Point Is Still Retained

Once the materials match up, the old source-code entry point is still useful. When opening `Source/Core/Layout/FlexFormattingContext.h`, first confirm that you are looking at the relevant flex stretch reference, rather than similarly named allocation code or other layout processing. What needs to be recorded is not a statement that "stretch calculated it wrong," but whether the size difference already existed before entering the reference and whether the same difference remained after leaving it.

You can follow the short branching flow in the old record:

```text
Aligned generated file and version
├─ The difference already exists before entering the reference
│  └─ Do not treat FlexFormattingContext as the first place to modify
├─ The difference is unchanged between entering and leaving the reference
│  └─ Do not list stretch as the cause
└─ The difference first appears or grows near the reference
   └─ Save the locations before and after it as material for subsequent layout inspection
```

The last branch is not a confirmed conclusion either. It only indicates that the relationship between these nearby locations is worth investigating further. The old document did not retain samples sufficient to establish containing block, explicit height, or automatic minimum size individually as causes, so these terms remain only reminders: if the input and the records from before and after the reference are already available, you can check whether they played a part in the layout conditions for that run; if those materials are not available, do not list any of these items in the cause field.

An early version placed fallback path near the start of troubleshooting so the symptom would disappear from regression testing as quickly as possible. No successful examples of this action were recorded, nor were any conditions for its use. Now, if the materials are incomplete, the version is unknown, or the size difference has not yet been established before and after the reference, do not use this page as a basis for switching fallback path. Even if the sample has been reproduced, first save the generated file, the version, and the size locations before and after the reference; this old record does not provide a verified switching procedure.

## Build Log Notes

A later review added a clue: the input and output for the still-unconfirmed part were left in the CMake configure log. The log can help recover the materials left at the time, but the log itself does not establish a conclusion about cross size. When opening it, first check whether the input and output for this run can be matched within the same section of the record. If you find only one of them, return to the branch for incomplete materials; if both are present, cross-check them against the actual generated file and version.

An easy mistake to make here is to see a similar name in the log and take it to be the result from that optimized flex stretch cross size run. Similar names can only suggest where to look, not establish a match among the file, input, and version. If the input or output in the log does not match the file at hand, stop at the build-side discrepancy, and do not skip past it to make the layout reference the target of a fix.

The log also cannot replace a rerun on a platform supported by the maintainers. It preserves the input and output clues left at the time; a rerun produces the actual artifact to be compared now. When both are available, they can be used to confirm whether this review connects back to the original case. If you have only the log and no generated file that can be checked, you still cannot say the anomaly has been reproduced; if you have only a generated file but cannot find the log, you need not make the converse inference that the log must be missing something, and should simply record the available materials.

## Record This Separately from Related Issues

There is also a record about fractional flex item distribution in the flex layout area, with the relevant entry points at DOC-21. If you see fractional distribution, rounding, or item distribution behavior, you can follow that issue thread; but do not turn this page's cross size record into a fractional distribution issue just because both occur in the same kind of layout. The focus here is the cross size before and after the stretch-related reference, still on the condition that the file being compared, the input, and the version have already been aligned.

Similarly, seeing containing block, explicit height, or automatic minimum size does not automatically turn the sample into a different class of anomaly. These appeared very early in the old record, making it easy to assume that the path was already established. In practice, return to just two questions: whether the difference already existed before entering `FlexFormattingContext.h` or changed near this reference; and whether the file under investigation really came from the verified input and version. If neither question can be answered, stop at the recordkeeping stage.

## What to Leave for Handoff

If the file generated by the rerun differs from the file under investigation, record the mismatch and any identifiable version relationship, and do not go on to write conclusions about stretch. If the files match but cross size is no longer abnormal, retain the file and version from that run; the earlier symptom cannot therefore be attributed directly to stretch. If the files match, the version matches up, and the anomaly is still visible on a platform supported by the maintainers, then save the size locations before and after the reference so that subsequent inspection can start there.

AUR-208 can still serve as navigation points for this review, with one unconfirmed item retained there. This is not the same as an instruction to modify the layout. The value of the old version lies in the initial source-code location it recorded and the cautious ordering expressed by "do not change fallback path first"; the later checks of the generated artifact, version, and CMake configure log were added to keep an unaligned sample from entering that narrow path.
