This record was initially tucked into the Geometry Bridge closeout to-do list. `fractional table tracks` was interpreted at the time as an update to the maintenance entry point: platforms and versions needed to be checked in the current build configuration, with any missing items then recorded in configuration files. This reading was convenient in one respect, since it allowed tasks to be broken out immediately; it also left a problem, with the meaning of table tracks, the scope of the configuration checklist, and the source-code entry point all written into the same sentence.

The initial draft made no further assertions about this. The stable reference point given in the old investigation records was `Source/Core/Layout/TableFormattingDetails.h`. The first decision was therefore narrow: retain that path as a verification entry point, and keep configuration checks as a separate matter. Having Table and Formatting in the path was not enough to show that it owned the entire implementation, nor enough to prove that every build target would pass through the same place. These two limitations were not made very clear at the time, making it easy for later readers of this page to mistake an "entry point" for "ownership."

## How the Initial Draft Handled It

Three approaches were discussed at the outset.

The first was to classify `fractional table tracks` entirely under build configuration. This option came from the maintenance task: platforms and versions needed to be checked, and missing items needed specific configuration files in which to be recorded. It was suitable for organizing the pre-release workload, but could not answer which quantities in table layout would form fractional tracks. Configuration records describe the scope of use, not the rules for tracks. Combining the two would lead later readers to think that filling in a configuration item also completed the layout-side check.

The second was to assign the item directly to `Source/Core/Layout/TableFormattingDetails.h`. This was closer than the first option to the layout object indicated by the name, but the records available at the time were only sufficient to link the old issue name and call name to this location. The file location provided local declarations and navigation to adjacent code, not a map of implementation responsibilities. If it were documented as the sole owner, later readers seeing neighboring paths would lose their reason to check further.

The third was to keep the two matters side by side: continue checking platforms and versions on the configuration side; on the layout side, start from that file to confirm local declarations and their adjacency relationships. The initial draft adopted the third option. It was not a decision about the specific way a fractional track is calculated, but a decision not to let a release task replace verification of a layout issue.

The cost of this decision was also straightforward. Readers could not determine completion from the task alone, but had to distinguish "whether the configuration item is listed" from "whether the track relationships have been established." There were no additional records at the time to support collapsing these two statuses into one conclusion, so no unified completion criterion was set.

## The Earlier Judgments Remain

The initial draft contained an implicit judgment: once platforms and versions were recorded in specific configuration files, the maintenance entry point would count as complete. This statement is still useful for assigning work, but is no longer suitable as a conclusion about the track issue.

It was not deleted, not because it remained accurate, but because it explains where the subsequent review began. Configuration files are where missing items belong; table tracks are not another name for configuration files. Both appeared in the same round of closeout work, which caused the early wording to blur them together.

Another earlier judgment was "the path is enough to point to the implementation." Here, "point to" was later used in a weaker sense: it means that the old investigation records can lead to a local source-code entry point, not that the complete call chain has been confirmed, nor that the file is responsible for all behavior. This revised interpretation was retained so the old records would not be read as having already established which code was responsible.

The configuration task in the initial draft was not withdrawn during the review. It remained an actionable part of the maintenance checklist, but could no longer carry any broader meaning. The early records placed "adding missing entries to configuration files" right next to "confirming table tracks," so readers would naturally treat the latter as the result of the former; this was precisely what later needed correction.

## Boundaries Identified During the Review

The review did not add a complete description of table behavior, but instead redrew the boundaries of what the existing material covered.

`Source/Core/Layout/TableFormattingDetails.h` can support two limited types of work. First, checking whether local declarations related to table formatting are still near that entry point; second, continuing the investigation along adjacency relationships rather than drawing conclusions from the name. It cannot, on its own, support checks of platforms, versions, or the scope of use in builds. That latter type of information still needs to come from specific configuration files.

Conversely, build configuration can only answer questions about what it actually lists. A platform or version appearing in the configuration means that it is within the scope of use to be checked; no records support extending that fact to mean "all fractional track scenarios have already been verified on that platform." The wording of the earlier tasks was terse, making it easy for readers to supply that meaning themselves. Separating the two here does not add process, but puts the two previously conflated questions back in their respective places.

The state relationships drawn at the time are shown below. They express the verification paths split out from the maintenance item, not a description of the table track algorithm.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Maintenance item" as Entry
    state "Configuration check" as ConfigCheck
    state "Layout entry-point verification" as LayoutCheck
    state "Unconfirmed" as Pending
    [*] --> Entry
    Entry --> ConfigCheck : Platforms and versions
    Entry --> LayoutCheck : Source-code entry point
    ConfigCheck --> Pending : Does not replace track verification
    LayoutCheck --> Pending : Insufficient adjacency relationships
```

The decision after the review was therefore: continue treating `fractional table tracks` as something that needs to be verified starting from a layout entry point; checks of platforms and versions in the build configuration are no longer treated as substitute evidence for it. If the maintenance checklist needs to retain this work, it should also clearly state whether a configuration item is missing or something near the layout entry point remains unconfirmed, rather than simply saying "tracks have been handled."

This decision does not define the algorithm for a fractional track, nor does it claim that all table scenarios share the same path. When the old page is cited, what can be recovered here is the boundary between verification activities, not a current behavioral specification.

## Counterexamples Separated the Issues

One common misreading deserves its own mention. Some readers saw "check platforms and versions in the current build configuration" and took the issue to mean that table tracks were not enabled on a particular platform. This inference skips an intermediate layer: the task only called for checking platforms and versions and identifying configuration-file locations for missing items, and did not record any platform's track behavior or a direct relationship between a switch and tracks.

There is another misreading: since the old investigation records link the issue name and call name to `TableFormattingDetails.h`, all subsequent issues can be assigned back to that file. This turns a navigation clue into a responsibility boundary. A path can narrow the scope of investigation, but cannot replace confirmation of the actual adjacency relationships; especially when build configuration and layout objects appear together, this simplification recombines the two types of gaps.

These two counterexamples show why the middle approach adopted in the initial draft should still be retained. It is not elegant, and cannot directly provide a "completed" label, but it avoids two opposing forms of over-attribution: reducing a layout issue to a configuration item on one side, and pushing a configuration issue back into a layout entry point on the other.

## Reorganization Options Not Adopted at the Time

During the review, rewriting the entire record as a complete description of table layout was considered. This was not done. The existing material did not provide track allocation steps, numeric conversion rules, or call order; forcibly filling those gaps would only make a historical record look more certain than its actual information justified.

Deleting all the earlier wording about configuration and leaving only the source-code path was also considered. This was not adopted either. Checking platforms and versions was the reason this item first entered the maintenance checklist, and deleting that wording would obscure why the old task appeared, and even more so why it later needed to be separated from layout verification.

The third rejected reorganization option was to attach an owner directly after the path. There were not enough records here to bring the file's local declarations, surrounding call relationships, and missing configuration items into a single scope of responsibility. For this record, retaining the entry point was more consistent with the granularity of the original decision than assigning ownership in advance.

## A Verification Sequence That Can Still Be Used

When consulting this page, first check whether the maintenance checklist refers to platforms, versions, or missing entries in configuration files. Those are configuration-side issues and cannot be used to verify table tracks.

Then start from `Source/Core/Layout/TableFormattingDetails.h` to examine local declarations and direct neighbors. The goal here is not to guess the scope from the filename, but to confirm whether the object referred to by the old investigation records still has a corresponding location in the currently accessible entry point.

If sufficient relationships cannot be established on either side, leave the status as unconfirmed. Do not rewrite "the configuration item has been found" as "fractional table tracks have been verified," or "the source-code entry point still exists" as "configuration coverage has been confirmed." Both conclusions go beyond the old records.

This sequence is a way to read the old material, not an operating procedure for building a new implementation. It is retained here because this page will still be opened as a historical entry point; readers first need to recognize the scope of the early judgments to avoid repeating the same misreading.

## Boundaries with Related Records

The same round of Geometry Bridge work left other discussions of numerical interfaces, but this page does not extend to those interfaces. The significance of `fractional table tracks` here is limited to how the table track item moved from the maintenance checklist to a local layout entry point, and why configuration checks and layout verification are not interchangeable.

Accordingly, this page does not combine numeric rounding, scroll ranges, or rendering geometry into the same decision. Even if they appeared at similar closeout stages, they require their own material and judgments. Piling related terms together would again create a false impression: as though a single Geometry Bridge rule already covered all objects.

This boundary also explains why the record still seems incomplete. It preserves a classification decision and a correction made after a review, not an overview of table formatting. If local call relationships that can be confirmed emerge later, they can be added on this page beside the corresponding entry point; if there are only new missing configuration items, they should remain on the configuration side, without turning the history into a lengthy implementation description.

## The Conclusions Retained Now

This page continues to retain the core decision from the initial draft: record configuration checks and layout verification separately. The former deals with platforms, versions, and missing entries in specific configuration files; the latter starts from `Source/Core/Layout/TableFormattingDetails.h` to confirm local declarations related to table formatting and their adjacency relationships.

Unlike the initial draft, the path is now described only as a verification entry point, with no implication that it owns the complete implementation; configuration checks are likewise described only as checks of the scope of use, with no implication that track behavior has been established. This correction has not removed the earlier wording, because that wording was precisely the source of the later misreading.

One issue that has not yet been separated out is: what wording should the maintenance checklist ultimately use to distinguish "missing configuration items" from "unconfirmed layout relationships." For now, the only requirement is that the two statuses not share the label "handled." Until new local records are available, no more fine-grained status names will be invented here.

# Scroll Extent Rounding Troubleshooting Tree

This review did not narrow the issue down to a single scrollbar-rendering problem. The assumption in the initial draft is still useful for deciding where to start: there may be a range discrepancy near the rounded scroll extent clamp, but it does not establish causation. Keep AUR-213 as the entry point for result discrepancies in the current version; field records still need to be saved separately.

First capture a pair of comparable records. Each record covers only one trigger action and one direction. Content changes, container changes, direct scrolling, and changes triggered through a public entry point must be documented separately; if the action order is unknown, mark it as unknown. Then put the scroll extents before and after the change side by side, and state whether the observation point is before rounding, after rounding, or whether only the final thumb range was observed.

Follow these branches in order:

1. If the scroll extent before and after the change cannot be obtained, retain only the trigger action, direction, and final behavior, and stop at the recording layer.
2. If the extent is unchanged but the thumb range changes, classify it as the display branch. There is no reason to modify the clamp at this point.
3. If the extent is unchanged but the render geometry changes, first record the geometry change's position relative to the trigger action; do not recast it as a range discrepancy.
4. When the extent changes between the pre-rounding and post-rounding observations, continue to save the inputs and results separately for horizontal and vertical.

Do not combine directions. If horizontal shows a discrepancy and vertical does not, that only means the current record covers horizontal; the reverse is also true. If both directions show behavior, but one is caused by a container change and the other by direct scrolling, they are still two records. Combining them into "bidirectional repro" loses the trigger conditions.

Container size changes are especially easy to conflate with rounding boundaries. After the container or content changes, the scroll extent may already be using a different input; the visual result that follows is not necessarily caused by boundary handling. For cases like this, preserve the sequence as "range before change—trigger action—range after change." Proceed to the rounding branch only when the ranges before and after rounding can be compared under the same input.

Code inspection still starts at `Source/Core/WidgetScroll.h`. Use it to confirm the local declaration in the current revision, then use it as the starting point for tracing to direct use sites. Do not treat similarly named declarations as the actual handling sites just because the issue name contains round, horizontal, or vertical. First confirm whether a use site provides range input or consumes the result after the range is formed; this determines whether subsequent records should go back to the input side or the result side.

Handle the public entry point separately. If it can be triggered only through an external entry point, record the direction and range before and after entering the entry point, then locate the direct site where it connects to WidgetScroll. If the direct use site can also trigger it, place the two records together; if it has not yet been reproduced, write only that the same result has not been seen so far. Do not directly attribute the external call's behavior to the local declaration.

Older records included a temporary adjustment: "after crossing whole-pixel, shift one value up or down." It only moves the observation point; it cannot answer when the extent changes. When restoring in the field, retain the original trigger action, direction, and ranges at both ends; the temporary change can be rolled back, but it cannot replace the original record.

When the discrepancy appears only as whole-pixel scrollbar offsets and the extent is stable, refer to DOC-26; do not expand it further into clamp handling on this page. Conversely, if a record also includes an offset, that does not mean the extent discrepancy should be handed off to DOC-26. First determine whether the range changed, then decide where the record belongs.

# Scroll Extent Rounding Troubleshooting Tree

"There's a little extra at the end," "the scrollbar is not flush with the edge," and "the position is wrong after dragging to the edge" are often written in the same feedback item. Split them apart first when handling them. This page only follows changes in scroll extent near rounding boundaries; visually similar thumb range or render geometry differences should initially be retained as adjacent phenomena. AUR-213 is the navigation entry point for result differences in the current version; it does not replace the inputs and results from an actual case.

The initial draft described the issue directly as local behavior of a particular clamp. That wording was later withdrawn: it collapsed the trigger action, direction, and call site into a single result, leaving records unable to show at which step the range changed. This old assessment is still retained because it explains why the investigation is layered first, not because the original handling should be restored.

Before starting, establish one rule: each record should cover only one trigger action and one direction. Changes in content, changes in the container, direct scrolling, and changes triggered through a public entry cannot share one set of before-and-after values. If the only information from the case is "a difference was seen after dragging to the end," and it is unknown whether the content or container changed first, record the sequence as unknown. Do not fill in the sequence by guessing.

The minimum record should include the trigger action, direction, scroll extent before and after the change, and whether the observation point was before rounding, after rounding, or only the final visible behavior. If thumb range or render geometry can be obtained, list them separately; if not, leave them blank. A blank value here is not a failure; it means that this case cannot separate the range change from the display change.

```text
Start: a range difference is seen near rounded scroll extent clamp
|
+-- Can scroll extent be obtained before and after the change?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   `-- Save the trigger action, direction, and final behavior; stop at the recording layer
|   |
|   `-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- extent unchanged before and after rounding
|       |   |
|       |   +-- thumb range changed
|       |   |   `-- Record the display branch; do not modify clamp
|       |   |
|       |   `-- render geometry changed
|       |       `-- Record the order of changes; do not classify it under extent
|       |
|       `-- extent changed before and after rounding
|           |
|           +-- Appears only in horizontal
|           |   `-- Save the horizontal input and result
|           |
|           +-- Appears only in vertical
|           |   `-- Save the vertical input and result
|           |
|           `-- Appears in both directions
|               `-- First confirm whether it was the same trigger action, then compare
|
`-- Does the change appear only at the public entry?
    |
    +-- Yes
    |   `-- Record the range before and after the entry, then continue looking for the direct use site
    |
    `-- No or not confirmed
        `-- Work back from known use sites; do not assign ownership based on the issue name
```

This branch is not asking you to fill every cell. It prevents two common shortcuts: writing "the range was truncated" when extent did not change but thumb range did; and assuming that rounding changed the range merely because the final geometry changed. The first kind of record should stop at the display branch; the second should first fill in the order of changes. Both may be related to scrolling, but neither provides grounds for modifying rounded scroll extent clamp.

A change in extent before and after rounding only means that the range layer is worth investigating further. It does not indicate which declaration, call site, or layout input caused the change. The record should retain both endpoint ranges for the same trigger action, rather than only saying "it becomes abnormal after crossing an integer." If only a conclusive description is left, the next review cannot determine whether it is looking at the value before rounding, the value after rounding, or a result that has already been consumed by another path.

The direction must be saved separately. horizontal and vertical both belong to scroll, but that does not mean their inputs or trigger conditions are the same. If a difference appears for one direction under the same action and not for the other, this can only form a single-direction record; do not write the direction where nothing appeared as having already passed. If there is one phenomenon for each direction, but one was caused by a container change and the other by direct scrolling, this also cannot be called a bidirectional reproduction. Retain the inputs, sequence, and ranges for each one first, then determine whether a common boundary exists.

Container changes and rounding boundaries are easiest to confuse. After the content or container size changes, scroll extent may first receive a different input; the visual result seen afterward does not necessarily indicate what the clamp did. Record this type of case as "range before change—trigger action—range after change." Only put it in the rounding branch when the ranges before and after rounding can be compared under the same input. When the sequence is missing, there is no need to guess whether the phenomenon was caused by the container, margin, or scrollbar.

Do not mix direct scrolling with container changes either. If the record comes from dragging or scrolling to the end, retain the action itself and the ranges before and after the action; if the range remains stable and only the position or thumb range changes, keep it in the display branch. A screenshot of one drag to the edge cannot replace a range comparison; it can only show that the final view differs from the expected one.

Code inspection starts from `Source/Core/WidgetScroll.h`. This location is suitable for confirming the local declarations related to scroll in the current revision and expanding from confirmed objects to direct use sites. First transcribe the objects actually seen and the adjacent calls; do not search by name and assume that round, horizontal, or vertical are on the same execution path just because they appear in the results. The current investigation needs to answer whether this use site passes the value to scroll before scroll extent has formed, or consumes the result after scroll extent has already formed.

If the location is before extent is formed, the case record should return to the input side: what was the trigger action, what was the direction, and at which step was the rounding observation obtained? If the location is after extent, the record should return to the result side: did the range change, did thumb range change, and did render geometry change? Both locations may need to be retained, but the latter cannot replace the former. A result where "the end looks wrong" does not mean that the step forming the range has already failed.

The public entry should be listed separately, not because it is inherently more suspicious, but because it may hide an intermediate change. If only the public entry can trigger the behavior, record the direction and range before entering it, then record the result afterward, and next find the direct location where it connects to WidgetScroll. If the direct use site can trigger the same behavior, keep the two records together. If the same result has not currently been seen on the direct path, write only that it was not observed; do not delete the public-path record or change it to ruled out.

The old notes also contain a simplification that is no longer used: after crossing whole-pixel, move the result up or down by one value to restore the display. This changes the observation point but does not answer when extent changed. When the same case is encountered now, do not use this action as a restoration method. First retain the original trigger action, direction, and both endpoint ranges; if a temporary change is necessary, it must be reversible and saved separately from the original record.

Some cases also mention scrollbar offsets. When extent does not change and the difference is expressed only as whole-pixel scrollbar offsets, do not expand the investigation on this page into a clamp investigation; DOC-26 preserves the entry point for the adjacent issue. Conversely, seeing offsets in a given record does not mean that the extent difference should be handed off to DOC-26. The two objects can appear at the same time; before routing them, first answer whether the range changed.

There is no need to attach a complete set of screenshots for a handoff. The fields below are enough for the next check to pick up the same set of inputs:

| Item | Recorded content |
| --- | --- |
| Trigger action | Content change, container change, direct scrolling, or public entry; note when the sequence is unclear |
| Direction | horizontal, vertical, or two separately recorded cases |
| Range | scroll extent before and after the change; add the values before and after rounding when available |
| Display | Whether thumb range changed, and whether render geometry changed |
| Entry | Confirmed direct use site, or only the public entry confirmed so far |

"Change" in the table is not a causal conclusion. It allows later review to continue comparing the same pair of inputs and results without mixing container changes, range changes, and display changes together again. Do not fill in unobserved values by guessing; leaving them blank is more useful than combining different observation points into one data set.

When the entry has reached around WidgetScroll but it is not possible to confirm where the value was formed, stop there. Put the local declarations actually seen, the direct use site, and this range record together for the corresponding module maintainer to verify. Do not cross this step and modify clamp directly, and do not infer a call relationship from a phenomenon in the other direction.

When a temporary handling appears to restore the display, return to the original record and check extent. If the original range difference remains and only thumb range or geometric position changed, the handling did not resolve the object covered by this page; revert the temporary handling and retain which layer it changed. If the range difference disappears but the input, direction, or entry also changed, this still cannot be called a confirmed fix; a before-and-after comparison under the same trigger action is still required.

Three types of comparable material are still missing: whether the value before rounding can always be obtained at the same observation point; whether horizontal and vertical can provide samples with the same input; and whether the range changes between the public entry and the direct use site. Until more cases are available for these questions, this is the stopping point.

# Whole-Pixel Scrollbar Offset Compatibility Notes

This page began as a very narrowly scoped migration note. whole-pixel scrollbar offsets was written in the issue-name field, with only a call name and `Backends/RmlUi_Vulkan/vk_mem_alloc.h` beside it. The approach at the time was to trace back through these two names, confirm that the person searching had returned to the same header-file fragment, and then keep the check in the original record.

That lookup route is still worth preserving. It shows where the old material began and helps people avoid objects with the same name or unrelated configuration sections. But it does not itself locate the implementation of the offset behavior, much less replace the visible result of a call. The old page did not record rendering coordinates, input conditions, or failure output; turning it into a finalized compatibility finding would add content that never existed in the original record.

The original intent of the old entry can be summarized as:

> If the issue name and call name lead back to the same block of declarations, retain this verification lead for now.

In the May context, "retain for now" matters. It is not synonymous with "already passed". During the follow-up check in October, AUR-214 added a requirement at the other end: one successful call and one failed call should each leave their own visible result. The old route thus went from being the sole endpoint to a lookup trail shared by both types of record.

```text
Old record
whole-pixel scrollbar offsets
        |
      Call name
        |
Backends/RmlUi_Vulkan/vk_mem_alloc.h
        |
    A block of adjacent declarations

Record retained after the follow-up check
Issue name ──> Call name ──> Declaration location
                         |\
                         | \── Visible result of a successful call
                         |
                         \──── Visible result of a failed call
```

The two branches from the declaration location in the diagram do not mean that the header file initiates calls to the scrollbar. They only mean that these three kinds of material need to be cross-referenced within the same compatibility check: the old names lead people back to the historical location; the call site provides visible results; an implementation relationship between the two is not filled in through guesswork.

## What to Preserve from the Old Location

In the file pointed to by the old path, a group of Vulkan memory allocation configuration declarations can serve directly as location anchors. They are grouped in the same block and provide a useful basis for determining that the search has returned to the old lookup area:

- Near line 1015 is the `pAllocationCallbacks` corresponding to `VkAllocationCallbacks`;
- Near line 1018 is the `pDeviceMemoryCallbacks` corresponding to `VmaDeviceMemoryCallbacks`;
- Near line 1043 is the `VkDeviceSize` pointer `pHeapSizeLimit`;
- Near line 1049 is the `VmaVulkanFunctions` pointer `pVulkanFunctions`;
- Near line 1074 is `VkExternalMemoryHandleTypeFlagsKHR`.

For the first four items, the declarations copied while locating them in the source are as follows:

```cpp
const VkAllocationCallbacks* VMA_NULLABLE pAllocationCallbacks;
const VmaDeviceMemoryCallbacks* VMA_NULLABLE pDeviceMemoryCallbacks;
const VkDeviceSize* VMA_NULLABLE VMA_LEN_IF_NOT_NULL("VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties::memoryHeapCount") pHeapSizeLimit;
const VmaVulkanFunctions* VMA_NULLABLE pVulkanFunctions;
```

These names serve only two purposes on this page. First, they let people tracing back later know whether they have reached the area where the old material stopped. Second, they show that this area describes neighboring configuration objects such as Vulkan allocation callbacks, heap size limits, and function tables, rather than confirmed scrollbar logic.

Do not record `pHeapSizeLimit` as the maximum scroll range just because it contains size limit, and do not put `pVulkanFunctions` into the scrollbar call sequence just because it is a function-table pointer. The available material provides no behavioral link between these fields and whole-pixel scrollbar offsets. Preserving the names and line locations during migration is more useful than adding a seemingly plausible relationship.

`VkExternalMemoryHandleTypeFlagsKHR` should also be retained as a location anchor in the same block. It helps confirm that the search has not strayed into another structure definition, but does not need to be tied to a successful or failed call sample. If the reviewer cannot find this group of objects near the old call name, mark the record as "old location does not match" rather than replacing it with a similarly named declaration.

## What to Migrate from the Old Record

The migration target is not the Vulkan configuration, but that overly brief compatibility-check record. The new record should retain at least the following four items together.

The first is the original issue name whole-pixel scrollbar offsets. Do not shorten it to "integer offsets" or "scrollbar deviation". The old material used precisely this term to connect to the call name; changing the name would make it difficult for later readers to tell whether they were recovering the same round of checks or another, seemingly similar geometry issue.

The second is the old call name. The available material does not provide the text of that call name, so no function or interface name can be invented for it here. If the name can still be found in existing records, carry it over unchanged; if the name has been lost, retain the fact that the "call name is missing" and keep the issue name and header-file location, rather than inferring a new caller from adjacent declarations.

The third is the declaration location. Keep it brief, just enough to let someone return to the same block. For example, the record could read "1015/1018: allocation callbacks; 1043: heap size limits; 1049: function table; 1074: external memory types". This is neither a summary of the header file nor a responsibility assignment table for these objects. It is simply where the old path stopped in the file.

The fourth is the visible result after the call. AUR-214 requires successful and failed calls to leave separate results, so the two types of sample cannot be combined into a single line saying "success and failure coverage completed". Each sample should retain its own call identifier and the behavior actually observed; on the success side, "field is nonempty" cannot replace the on-screen result, and on the failure side, "declaration not found" cannot replace the observed behavior either. The current material does not provide the specific contents of the two samples, and this page does not fill them in.

The old entry can be moved into the new record in the following order:

1. First, copy the issue name, old call name, and old path, keeping their original spelling.
2. Under the path, write only the location of the declaration block, without expanding on the rest of the allocator configuration.
3. Split the successful call and failed call into two entries, attaching the visible result from that invocation to each.
4. Beside the two samples, note which issue name and which old location they carry over.
5. If the call name or the sample for the other outcome cannot be found, leave the gap rather than filling it with source-code adjacency.

A record migrated this way adds a layer of behavioral comparison to the May note, without recasting the old location as the implementation location. For people still using the issue name to search historical material, the original route has not disappeared; for those who need to assess the compatibility behavior, the record is no longer just a few header-file symbols.

## When There Is a Sample for Only One Outcome

This type of check is particularly prone to overstatement when the records are organized. If only the visible result of a successful call has been retained, the record should explicitly say "success sample retained, failure sample not retained"; if only a failed call has been retained, state the reverse. Do not describe the available side as though both outcomes have been confirmed, and do not infer the missing side from whether a declared pointer is nullable.

If a result exists but the old call name is missing, the sample should still be retained. It shows that a post-call behavior was indeed observed at the time, but the old route has been broken. In this case, the path and that set of line locations can be attached alongside it as historical adjacency information, but do not claim that the sample has been proven by that header file.

When the declaration block can be reached but the two kinds of visible result are not available, there is no need to delete the entire record either. Just retain it as material with "old location only". A broken old path and missing samples are different problems: the former affects whether one can return to the location inspected at the time, while the latter affects whether visible behaviors can be compared. Lumping them together as a single "not passed" status loses the distinction needed for later follow-up checks.

## Restoring the Old Route

When the migrated notes cannot show where they started, the recovery sequence should return to the simplest trail: first look up whole-pixel scrollbar offsets, then look up the call name in the old record, and finally open `Backends/RmlUi_Vulkan/vk_mem_alloc.h` and check whether the area around 1015, 1018, 1043, 1049, 1074 is still the original cluster of adjacent items.

Once you have returned to the file, there is no need to read deeper to compensate for the lost behavioral records. Seeing `pAllocationCallbacks`, `pDeviceMemoryCallbacks`, `pHeapSizeLimit` and `pVulkanFunctions` only shows that the reviewer has landed near the configuration block recorded on the old page. The next step should be to recover the visible results left by the call at the time, not to reinterpret these declarations as evidence of scrollbar offsets.

Conversely, if the call samples are still available but the file location does not match the old record, do not replace the path just to maintain the connections in the diagram. The samples can remain on file as a record of the behavior observed at the time, while the path is retained as a lookup entry point that is no longer valid. This distinction is precisely why this page is still referenced: the old route may not be accurate enough, but it preserves a historical location that cannot be skipped when organizing the records later.

There is currently no material explaining at which layer the offsets are rounded, nor any material identifying this group of Vulkan declarations as responsible for scrollbar behavior. AUR-214 is the navigation entry point for filling in the visible results of success and failure; this page preserves the names and locations that should be carried over when migrating the old record, along with how to handle a break in the route.

# Source Entry Point Migration Procedure

This index was not retired when the entry point was renamed. It preserves Source · Performance Lab's migration approach at the time: the capacity baselines, resource curves, and regression diagnosis work around Source each had their own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. The old page bundled these items into a single entry-point path. People still used it later to find the first break in the chain, so the original index name and a few imprecise assessments have been left in place.

The entry point still points to `docs/adj-source/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. This location lists only source-performance-lab's old entry points, replacement locations, and callers still using it; explanations that could not be traced back were not turned into firm conclusions. It is not a migration directory for the entire runtime, nor does it track resource curves on behalf of neighboring projects.

## Approach used in the old page

The initial assessment was that continuing along `backend target` would mix the original and trial paths, and that `texture buffer` should be split out on its own. That assessment is retained here because all subsequent arrangements followed from it; it was once treated as sufficient reason to start the migration, but no list of all active callers was provided.

The replacement location was recorded as `containing block` at the time, and `anchor distance` was marked as a difference to recheck. In the old records, these names were more like location markers; they did not mean these were already stable interfaces. The old entry point, new entry point, and compatibility callers were supposed to be tracked separately. In practice, only some names and a note on what was observed during rollback were left.

```text
Before migration
  backend target
       │
       ├── Existing callers keep reading the original entry point
       └── Trial callers take a separate path through texture buffer

Trial destination in the old page
  texture buffer ──> containing block
                       │
                       └── Return to the old entry point if an anchor distance mismatch is found
```

The diagram above is an excerpt from the old steps, not a structural diagram reconstructed later. It also explains why a new entry point appearing in the directory cannot, by itself, count as a completed migration: the directory only shows that a location was written down, not that a caller still in use has left the old path.

## Migration sequence at the time

1. Use this index to find the old entry point, and first record the caller to be migrated along with the capacity baseline, resource curve, or regression diagnosis it is looking at. The old record did not require migrating everything in one pass, nor did it combine these items into a single result.
2. Choose just one caller for the `texture buffer` trial path; do not both switch entry points and interpret the resource curve in the same round. Keep the old entry point readable so the original input can be revisited.
3. Once the trial path reaches `containing block`, continue comparing results from the same caller. The old page also required recording the second read, rather than keeping only a cleaned-up final state.
4. If `anchor distance` does not match, restore the old entry point, then check again with the original input. Here, "restore" originally meant only rolling back the entry point; the old page did not establish that other adjacent settings should be restored along with it.

This sequence was once used as guidance for a limited-scope migration. It also had a gap: the page did not list all consumers in `compatibility window`. The old draft made "split out `texture buffer` first" sound like a sufficient condition for completion; that wording is retained so people who later follow the old link can understand why work continued at the time, not to recast it as a verified conclusion.

AURA-015 records a check with a real consumer: it followed the original entry point through to the current revision and stopped at the first difference. This check made the old inference that "the caller had already migrated" untenable, but the card did not add a complete list of consumers or replace the migration sequence in this index.

AURA-018 only notes that the results for the current revision from the second read or run are missing. The old steps required checking the state on the second pass, but no corresponding result was captured, leaving this path incomplete. Do not interpret the missing second record as an absence of differences just because the replacement location was seen the first time.

The material from the two sides has not been merged here: this page retains only Source's entry points and caller-tracking method. AURA-012 also requires one replay using the old exit criteria to check whether it is still possible to stop safely; this refers to the stopping point after the old entry point is restored, not to a new migration plan.

## Parts of the old page that can still be followed

If a caller can still read the required object only through the old entry point, do not delete the records on the `backend target` side yet. Find that caller before migrating, and during the trial switch only to the replacement location listed in the index; return to the old entry point if `anchor distance` does not match. With the old path left in place, keep recording capacity baselines, resource curves, and regression diagnosis separately; do not collapse them into a single status in one migration table.

This page has no answer as to which callers are still on `compatibility window`. # Postmortem: Unmerged Source Version Records

The issue appeared at the record entry point for Source · Performance Lab. The current-revision records for two revisions had been placed under the same entry point; the records could still be opened, but the entry point itself did not identify which version was being read. The first observed discrepancy was a texture buffer mismatch with the old record. At that point, all that was known was that the results differed; the difference could not yet be attributed to record content, entry-point switching, or changes to the fallback path.

The main impact was on review and replay. The old record had not disappeared, but the entry point presented two current records in succession that should have been separate. Anyone starting a comparison directly from the entry point would mistake results from different revisions for before-and-after changes in a single record. No wider adoption was confirmed at the time, so neighboring projects, other source-performance-lab inputs, and peripheral services were not listed as affected.

## Initial Assessment

When the texture buffer was first seen to differ from the old record, attention focused on the result itself, and the assessment was that "the record content had changed." This assessment was made without first checking the revisions under the entry point or retaining enough context to identify which record the comparison belonged to. It could explain the observed difference, but not why the old and current records were both accessible from the same entry point.

Only after further inspection was it confirmed that the same entry point held the current-revision records for two revisions. The earlier speculation about changes or degradation in the resource curves then stopped: with record attribution unclear, differing results could not directly establish that the performance lab's target had changed. What was rejected here was the attribution, not the texture buffer mismatch itself; that mismatch was still what had actually been observed at the time.

## Sequence of Events

- **Discrepancy found**: The texture buffer seen during review differed from the old record. Because the entry point still appeared usable, checking for mixed versions was not initially a priority.
- **Entry-point state identified**: The current-revision records for two revisions appeared side by side under the entry point. The old record had not been replaced; it was presented alongside another version as a record that could still be read.
- **Retries stopped**: Repeated retries against the same entry point did not continue. Retrying would only return another result that could be opened but whose revision could not be reliably identified; the final line of green output could not prove that the two records had been separated again.
- **Evidence retained**: The state at the time was preserved in `docs/adj-source/incidents/Source-performance-lab-two-version-records-not-merged.md`. The file was retained to preserve the mixed-version entry point as observed, without overwriting the old record with what looked like a single current record.

Stopping retries narrowed the scope; it was not a fix. What could be confirmed at the time was that the entry point mixed records from two versions. It could not be confirmed that every read would return the same content, nor could the results after retries stopped be used to infer when the entry point started mixing them. Further review needs to identify the revision of the record being viewed first, then associate the results with the corresponding version for comparison.

The on-call handoff was updated with version information, request context, and stop conditions to avoid assessing recovery based only on the last successful read. The request context was used only to mark which read attempt that observation belonged to; it did not provide the fallback path's trigger conditions or fill in the missing timing information.

## Recovery Assessment

The compatibility window can restore a usable comparison window, allowing reviewers to handle the record they are viewing and the old record separately. Recovery here means only re-establishing a basis for comparison in which the records can be distinguished. It does not mean that the cause of the texture buffer difference has been established or that every place that might use the entry point has been verified.

The window was not documented as a complete adoption inventory. The available material does not establish the range it covered, when it became usable, or whether every read method would go through the same window. The compatibility window therefore cannot be documented as a completed full recovery, only as a basis for comparison that was usable at the time.

The fallback path was raised during the incident, but the reason for its change remains unknown. There is no material showing when it changed, which input triggered it, or whether it was the reason the two revisions were not merged. Documenting it as the root cause would turn a branch that has not been reproduced into a conclusion, so this remains unresolved.

## Gaps in the Record

- No usable timestamp is available for when the two revisions began appearing under the same entry point.
- The texture buffer comparison lacks context that clearly identifies the revision.

# On-Call Procedure for Failed Source Runs

This record is still organized around a single failed source-performance-lab run. The sequence in the old version was to find the current entry point first, then stop at the first difference; handling for screenshots, handoffs, and reproduction was added later, but the earlier assessments were not rewritten as confirmed root causes.

When a report comes in, preserve the run evidence first. Here, "run evidence" refers only to this run's original input, the version used at the time, and the first visible result, not green results from later reruns. If these are already incomplete, simply record what is missing rather than fabricate a starting point that looks complete.

## Preserve the First Result First

1. Access the project's own records through `docs/adj-source/runbooks/Source-performance-lab-one-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. First check the `visibility transition` preserved on the page, then the first `regression trace` that appeared. If the two were not both preserved, use the earliest failure as the stopping point.
2. Save the state as-is, the original input, and the current version. Do not restart immediately just because the UI is still responsive, and do not refresh permissions or regenerate data; record those actions together with their results only when the actions themselves are the conditions you intend to test.
3. A screenshot without provenance cannot serve as run evidence on its own. First recover the entry point and account that produced the screenshot; if you cannot obtain them, mark the current entry point as supporting evidence, and note the screenshot's missing provenance beside the original step.

The old version treated "clean up first, then check again" as a shortcut, but that approach is no longer used. A green result after cleanup only shows that a green result could be obtained later, and cannot overwrite the first failure observed.

## Stop the Comparison at the First Difference

When using the most recent normal sample for comparison, change only one condition at a time. First confirm whether both sides still point to the same current entry point, then compare the original input, version, and first visible result. Do not adjust multiple conditions at once in the same round and then infer the cause from the results.

- If the difference occurs before `visibility transition`, preserve the entry point and version, and stop the comparison.
- If the difference occurs at `regression trace`, leave the trace at the first failure; do not replace it with output from the second run.
- The old page had `display scale`, `cross size`, `fractional track`, and `scroll extent` written in the margin. These terms may be retained with the run evidence, but they cannot be used to declare that a particular condition caused the failure.

The output of this step is not a conclusion, but a record that lets the next person locate the first difference. Keep untested combinations marked as unknown, and do not treat the default configuration as a normal sample.

## When the Scope Extends Beyond the Lab

If the comparison has already moved beyond the scope of "failure samples, regression tiering, and instability-signal attribution built around test; with independent scheduling, maintainers, and exit criteria", do not keep stitching external observations into this run. Preserve this project's entry point and the observations already made, and hand them over to the shared interface's maintainer; the original project still handles user communication.

The absence of `resource owner` is also a stopping condition. The old version said "wait for an owner to appear before continuing", but during actual handoffs that often never happened. Now the only requirement is to find someone to take over through the original entry point for the current revision; if long-term responsibility has not been confirmed, leave it blank rather than assign ownership on someone else's behalf.

This also explains why restoring service does not mean the root cause has been confirmed: service may already be restored while the first difference, associated entry point, or person taking over is still missing. Keep the old statements in their original time context rather than turning them into definitive conclusions as of today.

## Notes Added Beside the Steps Later

AURA-002 are used to locate the first run on the current revision after the current entry point changes. Later green results cannot overwrite that run; in one handoff, someone replied to the previous record rather than this card, so confirm which run you are looking at before taking over.

AURA-005 require a second colleague to reproduce the failure using only the materials on the on-call page. Any prerequisites, inputs, or entry points that the person reproducing it cannot find should be marked directly beside the original step, not written up in a separate explanation. This records what is missing from the on-call page itself, rather than guesses supplied from elsewhere.

The handling for AURA-008 is more limited: after receiving confirmation, change only the corresponding field, and retain the original state of adj-source. For a while, no one could verify the action that was due on that occasion, showing that "someone saw the message" is no substitute for confirmation; record only the confirmations received and the actions that could not be verified in the on-call log.

AURA-011 remain an unresolved handoff entry point. If no one can be found to take over the current revision, leaving it blank is more useful than entering a temporary name. AURA-014 cover the case of a screenshot with missing provenance, which should be treated as supporting evidence as described above, not expanded into a complete run record.

## Handoff Contents

At handoff, leave a record of the actions taken, hypotheses ruled out, the owner that `anchor distance` pointed to at the time, and the time of the next check. If `anchor distance` contains only a name from an old record and no current entry point, accurately describe it as an old record as well, rather than using it to infer a new assignment of responsibility.

The next person takes over from the same step: first confirm whether the original input, version, and first result are still available; if they are, continue comparing up to the first difference, and if not, stop rerun-based troubleshooting and fill the gaps first. Each maintainer should respond only for the part they are responsible for, to avoid merging user communication, shared interfaces, and the lab's run evidence into a single conclusion.

## Legacy Fallback Section Still Retained

The old entry point and return actions have not been removed. With different permissions, the next shift may still need them to verify which entry point was used at the time; however, they do not prove that the recovery actions have been verified. `package root` and `compatibility window` were also once noted in the margin, and should be added to the run evidence only if they reappear in this run, not treated as routine checklist items.

This page stops at the failed run's current entry point, first difference, and handoff point. When modifying specific fields, change only the corresponding fields as confirmed; leave unconfirmed long-term responsibility and untested combinations where they are.

The primary impact here was that assessments were mixed together, rather than all visual differences being attributed to the same issue.

| Stage | Evidence left behind | What could be concluded at the time |
|---|---|---|
| Initial discovery | One entry showed current records for two revisions | containing block differed from the old record |
| Preserving the evidence | Preserved the version seen at the entry and stopped overwrite-based retries | A later successful state could not replace the original input |
| Partial recovery | selection box could be recovered | One user path recovered; this did not mean the cause was known |

```text
  `-- current record for the later revision

The entry itself does not say which branch was read.
```

Historical versions can remain in the archive for later review; this incident occurred at the usage entry, where both revisions appeared as current content. The page placed them together, but did not put the old assessment, later changes, and unconfirmed scope back into their respective time contexts. As a result, readers could easily form an explanation that seemed continuous but in fact had no continuous basis.

The early observation that "containing block differed from the old record" should still be retained as an observation. It shows that there was an inconsistency when compared with the old record; it does not show that containing block was the starting point of the entry's co-mingling, nor that it caused the change in scroll extent. If the two were previously linked into a single geometry issue, that merely connected adjacent phenomena into a causal chain; the existing material is insufficient to support that step.

Preserving the version seen at the entry and stopping further retries also does not mean that a usable old version had already been found. This action only prevented a refresh, rewrite, or a later normal result from erasing the initial mixed state. The postmortem needs to preserve both "what was first seen" and "what it later became"; otherwise, after the selection box recovered, the page would look as if two versions had never appeared side by side.

Recovery and explanation are two separate things and cannot substitute for each other.

AURC-006 is the workstream for validating the actual consumer through the original entry. The card's goal is narrow: find one actual consumer, read the current revision through the original entry, and stop at the first difference. It does not provide a complete list of consumers, nor does it place everyone who reads the entry in the same impact scope.

This validation left one important limitation: one execution record belongs to the previous version, while the current result has no source attached. The fact that the two items appear near each other on the same page does not mean they came from the same revision. If the current result were directly linked to the execution record from the previous version, readers would assume that the later result continued from the old input, or that the old record had been proven invalid by the current result. The existing records support only "the source was not attached"; they do not support filling in a source relationship for it.

Without an actual access record under a non-admin identity, we cannot interpret the failure to access the regular entry as the direct result of two revisions being co-mingled; likewise, we cannot say that the regular entry has recovered. AURC-011 and the recovery of the selection box cover different conditions: the former is an incomplete validation of the regular entry, while the latter is a partial user-path recovery that has already been recorded. Combining them as "the user has recovered" would conceal the gap created by the permission conditions.

The earlier account based only on a screenshot also did not resolve attribution. A screenshot can only show that a page fragment was saved at a particular time; it did not preserve the revision, entry context, and request record together, cannot explain why another path worked, and still less can it confirm whether the screenshot showed the old record or the later record.
